questions.question_text: Why does a directed network typically produce an **asymmetric** adjacency matrix?

options.text: A directed edge from $X$ to $Y$ creates an entry in row $X$, column $Y$, but not necessarily in row $Y$, column $X$
Directed networks always contain loops from a vertex to itself
options.why: Directed graphs do not necessarily contain loops.

options.text: The sum of edge weights in a directed graph must always be odd
options.why: There is no requirement that edge weight sums must be odd.

options.text: Vertices in directed graphs cannot have both incoming and outgoing edges
options.why: Vertices in directed graphs routinely have both incoming and outgoing edges.

questions.solution_text:
In a directed graph, an edge from $X$ to $Y$ only allows travel in one direction.
Row $Y$, column $X$ remains empty unless an opposite directed edge $Y\to X$ exists.
A directed edge from $X$ to $Y$ creates an entry in row $X$, column $Y$, but not necessarily in row $Y$, column $X$.
